title: Answer-Free Self-Referential Critics: Training Solve-Then-Judge VLM Judges with Preference Labels but Without Ground-Truth Answers

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable Solve-Then-Judge VLM critic training on preference-only datasets that lack ground-truth answer annotations. Paper [1] discusses self-training VLM judges without human annotations, which aligns with the same objective of training VLM critics without reliance on ground-truth annotations. Both aim to address the challenge of training VLM critics in the absence of annotated ground-truth data, making the purpose substantively equivalent.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, AF-SRC, extracts pseudo-labels from preferred responses to supervise the critic's self-solve step, replacing ground-truth supervision. Papers [4], [9], [15], and [20] describe pseudo-labeling techniques for training models without ground-truth data, but none specifically extract pseudo-labels from preferred responses to supervise a self-solve step in VLM critics. Paper [1] uses self-synthesized data for VLM judge training but does not employ the same pseudo-label extraction paradigm. Thus, the mechanism is not covered by prior work.

### Evaluation
The evaluation validates the method on a physical reasoning benchmark against an oracle baseline with ground-truth access. Paper [10] discusses evaluation without ground truth, using preference mining techniques, which matches the evaluation design of comparing against a baseline in the absence of ground truth. Although the specific benchmark differs, the evaluation design is substantively equivalent.

### Domain
The domain is vision-language model critic training. Paper [3] explicitly addresses VLM critic training, making the domain covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce shortcut behaviors caused by noisy preference-derived pseudo-labels. Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], and [16] all address issues related to noisy labels or pseudo-labels, but none specifically target shortcut behaviors like overfitting to option letters or permutation biases. Paper [7] investigates biases in LLMs, including option order sensitivity, but does not address pseudo-label noise or shortcut behaviors caused by it. Paper [24] discusses option symbol bias in multiple-choice question answering but does not connect this to pseudo-label noise. Therefore, no prior paper explicitly shares the same purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves group consistency gating, applying the self-prediction reward only when the model gives consistent predictions across option permutations. Paper [9] introduces a consistency evaluation metric for multiple-choice benchmarks, leveraging altered answer choices to assess response consistency, which is conceptually similar to gating based on permutation consistency. Paper [18] discusses self-consistency in internal reward models, which aligns with the idea of using consistency as a gating mechanism. Paper [27] explores permutation tests in regression models, but this is statistical testing rather than a gating mechanism. Paper [24] investigates option symbol bias but does not propose a gating mechanism based on permutation consistency. Papers [12] and [13] discuss self-rewarding mechanisms in VLMs but do not involve permutation-based gating. Thus, the mechanism is covered by [9] and [18].

### Evaluation
The evaluation reports improvements across metrics, including MCQ accuracy. Paper [9] uses multiple-choice benchmarks and consistency evaluation metrics, which match the evaluation design of this contribution. Paper [24] also evaluates multiple-choice question answering performance, focusing on option symbol bias, which aligns with the evaluation design. Paper [30] examines LLM sensitivity to option order in multiple-choice questions, which is consistent with the evaluation design. Papers [28] and [29] also evaluate consistency in multiple-choice tasks, using metrics similar to those in this contribution. Therefore, the evaluation design is covered by [9], [24], [28], [29], and [30].

### Domain
The domain is vision-language model critic training. Papers [8], [12], [13], [14], [15], [19], and [20] all work in the vision-language model domain, including training, reward modeling, and reasoning decomposition. While none of these papers specifically address critic training, they operate in the same general application area of vision-language models. Therefore, the domain is covered.
